strengths: RBMs are an important model and finding appropriate ways to train them is a topic of significant interest.

The paper highlights the phenomenon of critical slowing down and how pre-training the model with a low-rank approximation of the parameter matrix can help the model overcome some of the slowing down effects.
The paper is well-written and easy to follow.
It represents a pleasant read that is accessible to a broad audience.
The literature review and related work section read well and are exhaustive.
The idea of pre-training the RBM to encode the principal components is simple yet very effective.

Leveraging the analogy between critical slowing down and the struggle of RBM during training to be ergodic and discovering all modes of the distributions is elegant and intuitive (though I suppose this is not a novelty of this paper, it is very nicely pictured in the introduction).
The numerical experiments look solid and aligned with the theoretical insights given in the main text.
I have not thoroughly checked the mathematical details in the appendix, but at first glance, they look good.

The paper offers a novel contribution by proposing a pre-training technique and a new sampling approach for RBMs inspired by their thermodynamic properties. This builds on the existing theoretical analyses of RBMs.
To my knowledge, extending replica Monte Carlo methods to a learning trajectory is original and intriguing.
Including a specialized physics background in the Appendix makes the paper accessible even to readers without a physics background.
The idea of low-rank pre-training is interesting and seems like it could be useful if it scaled up.
The idea of doing AIS across the training run is creative and clever.
Parallel tempering across training steps seems new.
weaknesses: The paper suffers from a lack of clarity of presentation and lack of clarity of novelty.
The idea of a low-rank approach has already been used by others and it's unclear what novelty there is in any of the sampling approaches used after the pre-training phase.

There are notational inconsistencies and a general lack of clarity in terms of the main ideas; fundamentally the approach of fitting a constrained model seems straightforward and indeed there is a simple way to compute the projected distribution in the PCA space (using the Fourier integral representation of the Dirac delta function) which the authors do not discuss.
The RBM definition is introduced only near the end of page 4; it would be helpful to introduce the RBM formally earlier in the text.
Notation is inconsistent with the use of $N_v$ and $N_{\text{v}}$ throughout, similarly for $N_h$.
Equation 1: it might be better to write $W_{i\alpha}$ rather than $w_{i\alpha}$ since w is used later for the "singular values".
Figure 1 isn't very easy to parse; for example the panel on race is placed more in the Mickey column than the human genome column.
Please clarify the difference between "model averages" and "observable averages" and the difference between using $N_s$ independent MCMC processes and $R$ parallel chains.
Please clarify for the reader the meaning of <v_i h_a>_D.
Section 4: it is not correct that it is possible to train "exactly" an RBM with a reduced number of modes; approximations are required, as explained in the supplementary material.
State what the free parameters to learn are in equation 3; if u and \bar{u} are the singular directions, then the free parameters would be $w_\alpha$?
In general I found the description of the low-rank approach unclear and this important section needs work to make it simpler and more clear to the reader.
For figure 14 it would be useful to show the distribution of the PCA projected data to see how well the RBM matches the projected data distribution.

It is unclear what contribution the authors are claiming to make; they state that the learning of the low rank parameterisation of W has been done before. Please clarify what the contributions of the paper are.

I find it hard to follow why the authors are considering different sampling schemes and therefore what the aim of this section is; I presume this is considering alternative sampling approaches after the low-rank pre-training has been applied, but I struggle to follow a clear recommendation or conclusion as to which method might be more suitable.

In the conclusion the authors claim to have introduced a method that enables "precise computation of log-likelihood"; there is no experiment measuring the quality of the log-likelihood approximation, and evidence is needed to support this assertion.

The use of the term "mode" isn't very clear; the phrasing suggests that the first d modes of the maximum likelihood trained RBM should correspond to the d "modes" of the PCA solution, which is unclear.
The notation \hat{u} is confused with \bar{u}.
Why use $w$ here whereas $W$ is used in the main text?
The derivation is quite confusing; for example the dependence on \bar{u} in equation 7 disappears without explanation and \bar{u} seems to be never properly defined.
Please state clearly what are the parameters of the model that are being learned.
Section A.2: the claim of exact training is incorrectly made here.

Notation in equation 20 is confusing, such as $w_{\alpha,a}=\sum_i w_{ia}u_{i\alpha}$ – are arabic and latin indices meant to indicate referencing a different entity, even though both objects are labelled w?

The supplementary material is confusing; it appears to fit an RBM projected to the d-dimensional subspace defined by PCA of the data to the empirical data distribution in that same subspace, but approximations are required and the approach is not well explained and is somewhat misleading.

An alternative (and standard) way to compute the marginal $p(m)$ is to use the integral (Fourier) representation of the Dirac delta function; it is unclear why the authors do not employ this approach, which would involve fewer approximations.

It is difficult to identify the two main contributions in the paper as they are totally disentangled in their presentation between Sec. 4 and Sec. 5.2; a list of bullet points at the end of section 1 to clearly list the contributions would substantially help navigate the paper.

The structure of sections 5.2 and 5.2.1 can be improved; it is confusing that Parallel Trajectory Tempering is introduced in section 5.2 and Parallel Tempering approaches are discussed in section 5.2.1; a more natural flow would be to introduce Parallel Tempering first and then explain what makes PTT different.

The discussion around eq. (4) is crucial; the novelty with respect to Decelle and Furtlehner (2021a) is not very clear and the authors should elaborate more on this, including intuition behind the "magnetizations" along each singular vector, the benefit of an augmented bias direction compared to the naive approach, and provide ablation studies comparing performances between Decelle & Furtlehner (2021a) and the new approach.

The distinction between theoretical claims and empirical findings is not clear; the authors should clarify which parts of the study are based on theoretical analysis and which are supported by numerical experiments, especially regarding equilibrium phase transition claims when updating parameters with limited samples.

In Section 4 the paper introduces pre‑training for low‑rank RBMs with SVD‑based weights to avoid continuous phase transitions and claims training can proceed quickly using PCD after post‑pre‑training; a more detailed explanation of this intuition is needed, and concerns remain that multiple stable clustered states may make PCD challenging and introduce bias.

The statement that highly clustered data is often ineffective because of first‑order phase transitions in EBMs raises the question of whether a first‑order transition in the learned RBM typically occurs regardless of the statistical model being learned; for example, does it arise when learning an Ising model without a local field?

The claim regarding first‑order transitions requires further elaboration; the cited phase diagram does not appear to show a first‑order transition and the AT line suggests continuous transitions, so validation by examining the free energy of the learned model would be appropriate.

If a first‑order transition does exist, the exchange probability in PT would approach zero near the transition; the authors should indicate whether this phenomenon has been observed and evaluate the round‑trip rate of PT and PTT.
While preparing models at different temperatures is challenging for PT, the proposed approach also requires storing models during the learning process.
The CelebA data in Figure 2 appears to be truncated.

The paper has a somewhat limited audience; it mostly builds upon work from a small group of authors, uses jargon familiar to that community, and relies on heuristic explanations that assume a statistical‑mechanical point of view.

Much of the motivation centers on "highly structured" data, which is not defined clearly; the paper does not show examples of the methods succeeding or failing in the presence of this structure, and the lack of a clear definition makes it difficult to assess the scope of the proposed methods.

The main text is highly verbose, with most concrete content in the appendices; nothing novel is introduced until page six, and core algorithmic contributions should be presented earlier and more concisely in the main text.

It is difficult to appreciate precisely what the contribution of Section 4 is; the insight appears to be "do Decelle & Furtlehner (2021a) before you do PCD", and the specific modifications or extensions to the D&F (2021a) method should be clearly delineated.

The ideas of Section 5 are interesting and Figure 3 is intriguing, but the empirical results are at the level of "preliminary findings" on a single small problem; the lack of experiments on larger datasets or more complex problems limits the impact of this section.
The title is too broad relative to what the paper delivers.
